title: Grilled Guinea Fowl
author: Fafa Gilbert
desc: A kilo and a bit of guinea fowl with five tablespoons each of suya spice and melted shea butter, finished with dried mint.
longDesc: Guinea fowl is the northern Ghanaian bird and this is the grilled version, rubbed with five tablespoons of suya spice mix and five of melted unrefined shea butter. Shea butter rather than oil is the northern choice and it is what makes this taste regional rather than generic. Dried mint leaves, two sliced onions, a teaspoon of chilli flakes, a teaspoon of vinegar and salt complete it. The method is video-only, so no grilling times or temperatures are published and the steps here are reconstructed and labelled as such.
ingredients: 5 tbsp suya spice mix (yaji) — see GHA064
5 tbsp melted unrefined shea butter, or coconut or groundnut oil
steps: // The published method for this recipe is video-only. No written steps exist in the source.
Joint or spatchcock the guinea fowl.
Combine the suya spice, melted shea butter, chilli flakes, vinegar and salt.
Rub the mixture all over the bird and under the skin.
Marinate, covered, at least two hours.
Grill over moderate heat, turning and basting, until cooked through and well browned.
Scatter the sliced onions over the bird toward the end so they soften and char.
Rest briefly, then finish with the dried mint leaves.
// The order and timings above are inferred from the documented grilled dishes in this collection, not from this source.
chefTips: Shea butter rather than oil is the northern signature here. It is nutty and slightly bitter and it behaves differently on a grill — it browns fast, so watch it.
Five tablespoons of suya spice to a 1.2 kg bird is a heavy crust and it is correct. Suya is meant to coat.
Dried mint at the end, not during. It is a finishing herb and heat destroys it.
Guinea fowl is tougher and leaner than chicken, so it needs a real marinade and moderate rather than fierce heat.
Be aware the method here is reconstructed. The author publishes a full ingredient list and no written steps or temperatures.
A teaspoon of vinegar in the rub is unusual and useful — a little acid helps tenderise a tough bird.
If you cannot get guinea fowl, use a free-range chicken and accept it will be milder. Do not reduce the spice to compensate.
commonMistakes: Treating the reconstructed step order as the author's own.
High heat, which burns the shea butter and the spice crust.
A short marinade on a tough bird.
sources: Quantities from 'Northern Ghana Style Smoky Grilled Guinea Fowl (Akonfem)', byline as printed 'Fafa Gilbert', 16 January 2019. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: 1.2 kg of Guinea Fowl; 5 tablespoonful of Suya Spice Mix (Yaji Spice mix); 5 tablespoonful of melted unrefined Shea Butter/ Coconut oil or Groundnut oil; Dry Mint leaves; 2 large peeled and sliced Onions; 1 teaspoonful of Chilli flakes; 1 teaspoonful of Vinegar; Salt to taste. NOTE that the dried mint carries no quantity.

METHOD GAP, stated plainly: THE METHOD IS VIDEO ONLY. No written steps, NO GRILLING TIME, NO TEMPERATURE and no doneness cue. The steps in this entry are explicitly marked as reconstructed and the step list carries a header saying so.

WHY IT IS PUBLISHED DESPITE THAT: shea butter as the grilling fat is a documented northern Ghanaian practice that appears in no other recipe in this collection, and all the main quantities are printed. Shea is to the north what palm oil is to the south, and a recipe that uses it deliberately is worth preserving even with an inferred method.

ON SHEA BUTTER, from Whitby 1968, 'Foods of Ghana': 'It is used for frying, for addition to soups and various other foods.' So its culinary use is documented across sixty years, not just as a cosmetic.
THE SUYA SPICE MIX this calls for is the same family as the tankora at GHA064, which is published with full quantities. The author gives no recipe for her own mix.
A SECOND RECIPE BY THE SAME AUTHOR, NOT USED: her 'Smoky Guinea Fowl & Spinach Soup', 16 November 2019, is Akan-style rather than northern and has no written method either.
ON GUINEA FOWL, from Whitby 1968: 'In the north guinea-fowls are almost equally common.' The GAIN 2016 Karaga District study adds that guinea-fowl eggs are those 'Usually' given to children.
NO YIELD is printed. The four servings above is an editorial reading of a 1.2 kg bird.
DRIED MINT in a Ghanaian grill rub is unusual and appears in no other documented recipe here. It is reproduced as printed.
reheating: A hot oven briefly, or back on the grill.
healthBenefits: Guinea fowl is leaner than chicken and higher in protein per gram.
Shea butter supplies vitamins A and E and stearic acid.
The suya spice contributes peanut protein, ginger and capsaicin.
culturalNote: Guinea fowl is the bird of northern Ghana — kept semi-wild, harder to catch and far better eating than chicken — and grilling it over coals with a suya crust and shea butter is how it is best served. The shea is the detail that places the dish: a southern cook would reach for palm oil without thinking.
